conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us spot common mood and anxiety symptoms that can crop up after childbirth, so we can make sure you get the right support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety—and then we’d talk together about any extra help you might need. We’ll go through the questions one by one; just answer in your own words. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Lately I’ve noticed it’s pretty hard to find things funny. I’ll smile if someone cracks a joke, but it feels forced. Most of the time I’m just too tired or worried to really laugh. Maybe once or twice this week I actually chuckled, but it’s definitely not like it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can laugh a little, but it doesn’t come easily—maybe a couple of times in the past week. Mostly it feels like I’m just going through the motions, and the joy doesn’t really stick.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, I haven’t been looking forward to much. When I think about the day ahead, it just feels like a list of chores—feeding, changing, trying to get the baby to nap. I used to get excited about little things like a walk with friends or even a favorite show, but now it’s like, “What’s the point?” I did manage to meet a friend for coffee two days ago, and for a few minutes I felt a flicker of “this is nice,” but it faded fast.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes… I do that a lot. If she won’t settle or I can’t figure out what she needs, my head immediately says it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m just not a good enough mom. Yesterday she cried for almost an hour and I caught myself thinking, “Any other mother would know how to soothe her; why can’t I?” I know it’s probably not fair, but the guilt keeps popping up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be holding her and suddenly picture her blanket covering her face or worry she’s too hot, too cold, not breathing right. My heart races and I can’t settle until I check on her—again. Sometimes I know it’s not logical, but the feeling just barges in anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a few times this week I’ve had that sudden “can’t-catch-my-breath” feeling, like something awful is about to happen, even when she’s right there sleeping peacefully. It hits out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to pace the hallway or grip the crib rail until it passes. There’s no real reason; it just shows up and then fades, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. I’ll be trying to make a sandwich and she’ll start crying, and suddenly it feels like the walls are closing in—dishes piled up, laundry everywhere, I haven’t showered, and I think, “I can’t do all this.” I usually still push through, but it feels like I’m barely treading water. Yesterday I just sat on the floor with her in my lap and cried because everything felt like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” about her, or I replay every little thing I think I did wrong that day. Even when she’s asleep, I’m wide-eyed, checking the monitor every few minutes. I probably fall asleep around 2 a.m. and wake up at five when she stirs. It’s not every single night, but more often than not.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that pretty much sums up most of my days. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Little tasks feel huge, and even when my family tries to cheer me on—"Look, she smiled at you!"—I just feel this dull ache inside. I’ll still care for her and do what needs doing, but it’s like I’m running on autopilot with this constant sadness humming in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week, yeah. It’s usually when I’m feeding her in the middle of the night and the house is quiet—I’ll just feel this wave of sadness and the tears start. Or yesterday, when she wouldn’t nap no matter what I tried, I caught myself sobbing into a burp cloth. It’s not all-day crying, but it keeps bubbling up, mostly when I feel overwhelmed or alone.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m tired and sad, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” sad most days  
- Markedly reduced pleasure/interest (anhedonia); brief flickers of enjoyment fade quickly  
- Daily tearfulness, middle-of-the-night crying spells  
- Excessive self-blame, “not a good enough mom,” guilt over infant crying  
- Unwarranted worries about infant safety, frequent checking  
- Sudden panic-like episodes (tight chest, shakiness) without precipitant  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “walls closing in,” difficulty completing basic tasks  
- Mood-related insomnia (racing thoughts, replaying events, 2–5 a.m. sleep window)  

<risk>Risk factors</risk>
- Multiple core depressive symptoms present most days for ≥ past week  
- Anxiety symptoms (GAD & panic-like) superimposed on low mood  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, household task paralysis, social withdrawal  
- No self-harm ideation (endorsed item 10 negative); no current safety concern

<obs>Screening observation</obs>
Patient’s responses are consistent with clinically significant postpartum depression with prominent anxiety. Frequency, duration, and functional impairment exceed “baby blues” threshold; further evaluation for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety disorder recommended.
